source: Weiser (1982) Programmers use slices when debugging, CACM 25(7)
finding: Founding claim: when debugging unfamiliar code, programmers mentally cut out slices, sets of statements linked by data flow, not contiguous text. Only the Crossref abstract was read; the full text and the exact statistics were not reachable (ACM returns 403, Tip survey PDF is a scan with no text).
numbers: Per Ko et al. 2025 retrospective (second hand): 2 programs of 75-150 lines of Algol-W, a few subroutines, variable names replaced by arbitrary single symbols, no comments. After each debug session participants saw relevant and irrelevant slices and recognised relevant ones more often.
quote: programmers also routinely break programs into one kind of coherent piece which is not coniguous
limits: Exact N and test statistics not verified this session. Tiny paper-sized programs, names stripped, recognition test after the fact, not a test that slicing tools help. Ko 2025 calls it a single suspect study with almost no later validation.
agent_relevance: O5 (work backwards from the failure) rests on this: relevance is a dependency subset of the code, not the whole file. Our agent can compute the slice with code instead of asking the model to guess it.

source: Ko, Myers, Coblenz, Aung (2025) A Retrospective on How Developers Seek, Relate, and Collect Information About Code, IEEE TSE
finding: Authors look back at their 2004 study. They describe Weiser 1982 as the start of two decades of slicing algorithm work, built on one small empirical study with almost no later validation. Their own data found developers build a fuzzy working set of possibly relevant code that approximates slices but is not a precise slice.
numbers: Weiser tasks: 2 programs, 75-150 lines. Cited from other work: developers spend about 24% of time navigating code (Xia et al.); 73% of context elements were structurally related.
quote: program slice computation had been catalyzed on a single suspect empirical study, with almost no later validation of their utility.
limits: Retrospective written by the original authors, so it is partly self-assessment. Numbers about navigation are second-hand citations.
agent_relevance: Warns that exact slices may be a wrong target. A soft, expandable working set of dependency-linked code may fit better than a strict slice. Use slice as the seed, then allow widening.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline: A Debugging Interface for Asking Questions About Program Failures, CHI 2004
finding: Prototype for the Alice language. The programmer picks a why did or why didn't question about program output from a menu, and the tool answers with a dynamic slice of the code responsible, shown on a timeline. Questions are phrased in terms of the visible failure, not runtime data or code lines.
numbers: Prior Alice studies: 68% of questions were why didn't, rest why did; 85% about a single object; 50% of all errors came from false assumptions in hypotheses formed while debugging. Menu content built from a database of all output changes plus precise dynamic slices.
quote: 68% of questions were why didn't questions and the remaining were why did questions.
limits: Alice is a small visual language with 3D worlds. Motivating numbers come from the authors' own earlier studies, not independent ones.
agent_relevance: Design pattern for the agent: ask questions about the failing output (why did this value appear, why did that not happen), let code compute the causal chain. Why-not is the larger share, so the schema must support absent events.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline, user study results (CHI 2004)
finding: Between-groups lab study: 9 CMU HCI Masters students built a Pac-Man game in Alice in 90 minutes, 4 without the Whyline and 5 with it. The Whyline group finished 40% more tasks and diagnosed identical errors far faster.
numbers: Tasks completed: with M=3.20 (SD .457) vs without M=2.25 (SD .500), t(7)=3.0, p<.02. Time from failure to diagnosis for six identical scenarios: F(1,5)=12.64, p<.02, average speed-up factor 7.8 (e.g. 330 s without vs 38 s with in the first scenario). The Whyline was useful for 19 of 24 questions; 0 of 3 for the first user and 5 of 5 for the fifth.
quote: programmers with the Whyline completed significantly more tasks (M = 3.20, SD = .457) than those without (M = 2.25, SD = .500)
limits: N=9 total, iterative design so the tool changed between sessions, graduate students, one small program, tool authors ran the study. Effect size likely inflated. First prototype lacked why didn't and the user said it was useless.
agent_relevance: Shows that the why-not question type decided whether users trusted the tool. Our agent should not skip the 'why did X not happen' path.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented: Asking and Answering Why and Why Not Questions about Program Behavior, ICSE 2008
finding: Java Whyline. Developers pick a question about output from the trace, and the tool uses static and dynamic slicing, precise call graphs, and an algorithm for why a line was not reached. Tools like breakpoints and slicers have a garbage-in garbage-out problem because the developer must first choose a line or variable.
numbers: Authors cite that developers' initial guesses were wrong almost 90% of the time. Question coverage: 8 of 9 sampled real bug reports on 5 programs had a matching question. Pilot slider-bug study: 9 Whyline users median 4 min (range 1-12) vs median 10 min (range 3-38) for 18 expert Java developers with Eclipse, p<.05 Wilcoxon rank sums. Traces of 35,597 I/O events navigable on ArgoUML. Unpublished: experts twice as successful in half the time.
quote: developers' initial guesses were wrong almost 90% of the time
limits: One task, 9 people compared to a control from a prior study (not randomised, not same time), novices vs experts, unfamiliar code. Authors say generality is limited. The 90% is from their earlier work, not independent.
agent_relevance: The 90% wrong-first-guess figure is the argument for O5: start from the observed failure and trace back before guessing a cause. Experts speculated first and checked, novices just asked the direct question and did better.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented, speculation behaviour note
finding: Novices said aloud 'Why is the line blue?' and asked the Whyline exactly that. Experts first speculated about possible reasons and then looked for a question that would test their speculation, asking about the output only after that failed. Experts did not believe the tool could link slider to colour.
numbers: Whyline group median 4 min vs 10 min control; most Whyline users self-described novices.
quote: It was like a treasure hunt! It was fun! I didn't know debugging was like this.
limits: Anecdotal observation from a pilot of 9, no coding of strategies reported. Could be about trust in the tool and not about expertise.
agent_relevance: A model that has learned expert-style habits may guess a cause first and hunt for confirmation. Schema should force the plain symptom question before any hypothesis, and then check the hypothesis against the answer.

source: Ko and Myers (2009) Finding Causes of Program Output with the Java Whyline, CHI 2009
finding: Controlled experiment, the best-powered Whyline test: 20 masters students in software engineering, 10 per group, Whyline vs breakpoint debugger, on two real ArgoUML bug reports (bugs 3121 and 3128), 30 minutes each.
numbers: Task 1: 10 of 10 Whyline users completed vs 3 of 10 control (chi2=10.6, p<.05); Whyline twice as fast (t=4.5, p<.05). Task 2: 4 of 10 vs 0 of 10 succeeded (chi2=5, p<.05); no speed difference (ceiling). Median distance to key function in the dependence graph was lower for Whyline in task 1 (t=4.6, df=18, p<.0002) and not different in task 2.
quote: Whyline users were successful about three times as often and about twice as fast compared to the control group
limits: Students, unfamiliar code, only two bugs, authors built the tool. Task 2 success only 4 of 10. Tool localized the bug but often did not help understand its exact nature. No industry experience effect found but sample too small to test.
agent_relevance: Strongest human evidence that asking about output and following dependencies beats the guess-and-breakpoint loop, at least on UI-output bugs. Supports O5 as a default for the agent.

source: Ko and Myers (2009) Finding Causes of Program Output with the Java Whyline, behaviour measures
finding: Whyline users relied on questions and avoided text search. The control group used breakpoints and text search and often read the buggy method and then wrongly judged it unimportant and never returned. Whyline users decided faster that a method was buggy and were generally right when they said so.
numbers: Task 1: Whyline users viewed fewer files per minute (t=22.6, df=18, p<0.0001) but similar files overall; task 2: more files per minute (t=2.2, df=18, p<.05). Median 4 why did questions in task 2. Why didn't questions: rarely asked, users got frustrated by analyses taking up to about a minute.
quote: Whyline participants tended not to ask "why didn't" questions and when they did, they tended to get frustrated
limits: Why didn't was barely used in the test tasks, so the benefit of why-not is not shown here (it was shown only in the 2004 Alice study). Possible loss of serendipitous knowledge noted by authors.
agent_relevance: Two lessons. Control group threw away the right method after reading it; the agent needs a record of rejected candidates with the reason, so they can be reopened. Slow why-not answers were avoided, so cheap checks should be offered first.

source: Ko, Aung, Myers (2005) Eliciting Design Requirements for Maintenance-Oriented IDEs, ICSE 2005
finding: Observation of 10 expert Java programmers in Eclipse on 5 maintenance tasks, 70 minutes each. Work was an interleave of collecting a working set of relevant fragments, navigating its dependencies, and editing. Much time was lost to navigation and to irrelevant code.
numbers: Mean 35% of time spent just navigating between dependencies (about 19 minutes); mean 46% of time inspecting task-irrelevant code; of 48 task starts, 40 began with a search, and only about half of those searches reached relevant code.
quote: programmers spent an average of 35% of their time simply navigating between dependencies
limits: N=10, single IDE (Eclipse 2.1 era), one observation lab. Programmers were interrupted on a fixed schedule; interruptions excluded from the 35%.
agent_relevance: Gives a cost model for repo debugging: the search for relevant code is a big overhead. A dependency-based slice or call chain cuts this overhead, which is the agent's version of the Whyline benefit.

source: Ko, DeLine, Venolia (2007) Information Needs in Collocated Software Development Teams, ICSE 2007
finding: Observed 17 developers at Microsoft, 25 hours, 334 instances of information seeking, 21 information needs. The two most often unsatisfied needs were about causes of program state and behaviour, which are the why questions. Developers often turned to coworkers because tools could not answer them.
numbers: Unsatisfied rates and longest search: 'What code caused this program state?' 61%, up to 21 min; 'Why was the code implemented this way?' 44%, 21 min; 'In what situations does this failure occur?' 41%, 49 min; 'What code could have caused this behavior?' 36%, 17 min.
quote: What code caused this program state?
limits: 11 of 17 teams were in a bug-fixing phase, which inflates debugging needs. One company, observational. Percent is of searches that were unsatisfied or deferred, not of all tasks.
agent_relevance: The questions an agent must answer most are exactly those that humans fail at: what caused this state, what could have caused this. Slicing from the failing state is the tool for the first one.

source: Shahandashti et al. (2024) Program Slicing in the Era of Large Language Models, arXiv 2409.12369
finding: Tested whether LLMs can compute static and dynamic slices of Java programs without tools. They are mediocre. GPT-4o was best. Exact-match slices were almost never right. A failure taxonomy found complex control flow as the top root cause.
numbers: 100 Java programs from LeetCode. Static slicing best Accuracy-D: GPT-4o 60.84% (one-shot CoT), exact match 7.33%; GPT-3.5 Turbo 46.43%; Gemma-7B 43.43%; Llama-2 17.57%. NS-Slicer (CodeBERT) 60.52%, exact match 0%. Dynamic slicing best: GPT-4o 59.69% (zero-shot), exact match 0%. Prompt crafting +4% and iterative feedback +3.9% on GPT-4o static slicing.
quote: the LLMs we experimented with are yet to achieve reasonable performance for either static slicing or dynamic slicing
limits: Short LeetCode programs, Java only, Accuracy-D is a lenient metric, their NS-Slicer numbers differ from the original paper, no comparison to a plain program-analysis slicer on the same set.
agent_relevance: Strong reason not to let the model hand-write the slice. Compute it with a real tool (G2: revise from real output) and give the result to the model.

source: Chang et al. (2025) SliceMate: Accurate and Scalable Static Program Slicing via LLM-Powered Agents, arXiv 2507.18957
finding: Three LLM agents (synthesis, verification, refinement) produce static slices without a dependency graph, and beat both traditional tools and learned slicers. Verification and refinement are what make the agent version work.
numbers: SliceBench: 2,200 manually annotated Java and Python programs of 5 to 8,577 lines. Reported gains over best baseline up to 63.1% accuracy and 62.5% F1 on large GitHub programs; average improvement 15.2% accuracy, 22.1% F1, 10.7% exact match. Ablation: dropping verification and refinement agents lowers F1 by 5.5% (Python) and 6.1% (Java) on small code, about 24.9% F1 on large code, and Accuracy-EM falls by 50%. In bug localization, IncBL with SliceMate uniquely found 56 bugs (BugsInPy) and 14 (Defects4J); LLM4FPM found 42 and 26.
quote: SliceMate significantly outperforms all baselines
limits: Authors built the benchmark. Baselines like Joern drop sharply on incomplete code, which favours the LLM. Counts of uniquely found bugs are not a rate and have no confidence interval.
agent_relevance: The slice is much better when a separate step checks conciseness and completeness. Matches our rule that the model proposes and code or a separate check verifies. Use as a fallback only when no parser can build the graph.

source: Wu et al. (2026) CausalRepair: Bridging the Causality Gap in LLM-Based APR via Dual-Slicing, ISSTA 2026, arXiv 2608.10613
finding: Feeds the repair LLM a minimal causal context built from a static slice of the failing test and an execution-trace dynamic slice of the source. Compared with 15 baselines using one backbone (DeepSeek-V3).
numbers: 313 correct fixes on Defects4J (V1.2 162, V2.0 151), 77 more than ReinFix (236), a 32.6% gain; 289 on Defects4J-Trans, 44.5% over state of the art; average cost $0.029 per bug. Ablation (correct fixes): without source dynamic slice 230 (-26.5%); without test slice, failing line only 193 (-38.3%); full test instead of slice 282 (-10.0%); no iterative repair 255 (-18.5%); no patch augmentation 260 (-16.9%).
quote: removing source-side dynamic slicing substantially degrades repair performance, reducing the number of correct fixes by 26.5%
limits: Single backbone model; Defects4J is likely seen in training (they add Defects4J-Trans to reduce that). Authors' own system and ablation. Too little context (just failing line) hurt most, so a slice that is too tight is worse than none.
agent_relevance: Best 2026 LLM number for O5: a dynamic slice from the failure beats static context by about a quarter of fixes, but cutting too much costs more (-38.3%). Slice, then check enough context remains.

source: Li, Su, Lyu (2026) From Laboratory to Real-World Applications: Benchmarking Agentic Code Reasoning at the Repository Level (RepoReason), arXiv 2601.03731
finding: Uses dynamic program slicing as a measuring instrument, not a tool. For each assertion-verification task the slice gives reading load (ESV), simulation depth (MCL) and integration width (DFI). Agents fail most when the slice has many independent upstream sources.
numbers: Accuracy falls below 40% for most models when DFI exceeds 20 independent upstream sources (Claude is the exception). Sharp drop once causally relevant code in the slice exceeds about 600 lines, and beyond 100 execution steps. DFI correlation with accuracy as strong as -0.234 (GPT-5.2). Per-repo accuracy ranged from 36.0% to 82.8% across seven repositories and six models.
quote: integration width serves as the primary cognitive bottleneck
limits: Mutation-generated assertion tasks, Python repos only, correlations are weak in absolute size (-0.234). Measures reasoning on a given slice, not whether using slices helps.
agent_relevance: Tells us where backward tracing breaks for a model: many parallel causes (fan-in over 20) and long chains. Agent should split a wide slice into sub-questions and cap a slice around a few hundred lines.

source: Pei et al. (2025) LLM as an Execution Estimator: Recovering Missing Dependency for Practical Time-travelling Debugging (RecovSlicing), arXiv 2508.18721
finding: Answers the Whyline-style question 'why does this variable have this value' (dynamic data dependency) from a partial trace, using an LLM to estimate the missing steps. This cuts instrumentation cost.
numbers: 8,300 dynamic data dependencies over three benchmarks: accuracy 80.3%, 91.1%, 98.3% vs best baselines 39.0%, 82.0%, 59.9%; recall up to 98.3% vs 53.4%, 79.1%, 87.1%. In a dual-slicing regression bug localizer it located 16% more regressions.
quote: answering the question of "why the variable has this value?"
limits: Needs a partially recorded trace; evaluated by the authors; abstract-level reading of the benchmarks only, the paper's larger body was not reviewed line by line.
agent_relevance: Shows a hybrid that is sensible for our agent: code records what it can, the model fills gaps, and the result is checked against the trace.

source: Zhong, Wang, Shang (2024) Debug like a Human: LDB, ACL 2024, arXiv 2402.16906
finding: Gives the LLM runtime values of variables after each basic block of the failing run and asks it to verify each block against the task, like stepping through breakpoints. Not slicing, but the closest LLM version of 'inspect the runtime state after the failure'.
numbers: Improves baseline performance by up to 9.8% on HumanEval, MBPP and TransCoder; new state of the art at the time for LLM code debugging.
quote: LDB consistently enhances the baseline performance by up to 9.8%
limits: Only function-level benchmarks with short programs; abstract-level numbers were read, per-model tables not reviewed. Later work (2611.09212) found trace gains inconsistent.
agent_relevance: Evidence that structured runtime state helps the model locate the fault. Pair it with a slice so the block list is restricted to the causal part.

source: Adnan and Kuhn (2026) On the Limits of Execution Traces for Repairing Assertion Failures in LLM-Generated Code, arXiv 2611.09212
finding: Limits result. For failures left after iterative repair, returning the program annotated with runtime values (Breakpoint Debugging) beat plain resampling on one benchmark, was close on another and lost on a third. A trace helps only if the visible failing input is enough to reproduce the fault.
numbers: BigCodeBench: 26.7% repaired vs 22.4% for resampling, gain grows with model size. HumanEval: BPD slightly better. LiveCodeBench: resampling 6.5% vs BPD 4.9%, and BPD gives no gain even on public tests. Unchanged-code resubmissions dropped from 28% to 8% on BigCodeBench. Tracing only the first failing test beat tracing all failing tests and used fewer tokens. Assertion failures are 79% of residual failures on BigCodeBench, all on HumanEval, 93% on LiveCodeBench (four Qwen2.5 models).
quote: an assertion failure says little about where the fault lies.
limits: Qwen2.5 family only, residual hard tasks, authors' own method. Argues that earlier trace results (2 of 6 configurations beat trace-free prompts) are mixed.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition on O5: a trace helps on logic bugs that the failing input exposes, not on spec misunderstandings. Trace the first failing test only. If trace gives no change, fall back to fresh attempts (G1).

source: Olausson et al. (2024) Is Self-Repair a Silver Bullet for Code Generation? ICLR 2024, arXiv 2306.09896
finding: Self-repair is bottlenecked by the quality of the model's feedback about why its code failed. A stronger model giving feedback, or a human giving feedback, raised repair gains a lot. This is the LLM version of 'it cannot answer why-questions about itself'.
numbers: Tested Code Llama, GPT-3.5, GPT-4 on HumanEval and APPS. When repair cost is counted, gains are modest, vary across subsets and are sometimes absent. Human feedback to GPT-4 in a small study beat model-only feedback.
quote: self-repair is bottlenecked by the model's ability to provide feedback on its own code
limits: 2023 models; the small human study had few participants (exact N not read from the abstract).
agent_relevance: Directly supports G2: the why must come from real output (slice, trace, failing test), not from the model's own explanation.

source: Weiser (1981) Program Slicing, Proc. 5th ICSE, 439-449
finding: Defines a slice as the minimal set of statements that could affect the value of a chosen variable at a chosen point, found by backward data and control dependency. Introduces the idea as a debugging aid, based on what programmers did when debugging.
numbers: No numbers recorded; PDF not reachable (ACM 403). Treated here as the formal definition used by the later studies.
limits: Not read. Known from citations: the static slice is large; later dynamic slicing (Korel and Laski) narrows it to one execution.
agent_relevance: Slicing criterion = (point, variable). For the agent: the failing assertion or wrong output is the criterion, and the slice is the set of lines worth reading.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline, question-type constraints
finding: Observed constraints on what programmers ask: they only ask why didn't about code that plausibly might have run; they phrase questions as 'why did Pac's direction change' (a failure) and not 'why is the value X now'. The design restricts the question menu to what the output could have been, which prevents assumptions about what did or did not happen.
numbers: 68% why didn't; 85% single-object questions (authors' prior Alice studies).
quote: By restricting the programmer's ability to make assumptions about what did and did not happen, we enabled them to observe and explore
limits: Authors' interpretation from observation; the benefit of restricting the menu was not tested alone.
agent_relevance: For the agent: restrict why-not questions to events that were reachable, otherwise the question space blows up. The code can build that menu (plausible-but-not-executed statements).

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented, why-not algorithm and cost
finding: The tool answers 'why didn't this line run' with static analysis of the call graph for the predicates that blocked it, then slices on those predicates at the time of the relevant event. Slicing criteria are chosen from the output by the tool and not by the user.
numbers: Trace sizes were reported for 5 programs (e.g. ArgoUML, 113,117 lines, 35,597 I/O events in a one-minute session); per-program overhead figures were garbled in PDF extraction and are not recorded here.
quote: all of these tools are subject to a `garbage-in garbage-out' limitation
limits: Overhead table not parsed; check source before citing.
agent_relevance: Formal model for O5: the question is first reduced to an event in the trace, then to the predicates that blocked it. The agent can do the same on test traces.

source: Ko et al. (2005) Maintenance study, false-hypothesis time and working set
finding: Programmers began tasks by searching for relevant code, and the search often failed. Of the searches only about half led to relevant code, and navigations to familiar code from previous tasks mostly did not lead to relevant code (only 2 did). The authors link the 46% irrelevant inspection to their earlier finding of false hypotheses in novice programming.
numbers: 48 task starts, 40 with a search; about 1/2 of searches reached relevant code; 2 navigations to familiar code were relevant.
quote: Programmers began each task by searching for task-relevant code.
limits: Counts are small; the sentence was cut at a line break in extraction so the exact wording after 'Of the 48 instances' should be checked in the source.
agent_relevance: Starting by keyword search is the human default and is half wasted. A backward step from the failing symptom replaces a blind first search.

source: Ko and Myers (2009) Java Whyline, limits and design discussion
finding: Authors list where it fails: the UI helped locate bugs but often did not help users understand their nature; the question menu is limited to observable output (UI, console, exceptions); static analysis for why-not is slow; users may lose serendipitous knowledge by following only dependencies.
numbers: Task 2 success only 4 of 10 even with the tool; why-not analyses on the order of a minute or less.
quote: One potential downside of the UI's focus on dependencies is that users may not find important or relevant code serendipitously.
limits: Qualitative discussion by the authors.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: the slice finds where, not why the programmer's logic is wrong. After localising, the agent still needs a separate step to explain the error and test the fix on held-out input (G3).

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline, scenario Table 3 contrast
finding: In the six matched debugging scenarios without the tool, participants hypothesised and diagnosed by inspecting and rewriting code; with the tool they hypothesised and diagnosed by asking questions and reading the answer. Same errors, different strategy, large time difference.
numbers: Mean speed-up factor 7.8 across the 6 scenarios (F(1,5)=12.64, p<.02); example: invariant 'why didn't Pac resize 0' answered in 38 s vs 330 s.
quote: the Whyline significantly decreased debugging time (F1,5 = 12.64, p < .02) by an average factor of 7.8.
limits: Scenarios selected post hoc because they matched between groups (many other scenarios were similar but not compared); six items, n small, the ANOVA treats scenarios as the unit.
agent_relevance: Selection of scenarios after the fact can inflate effects. Treat the 7.8x as an upper bound; the later 2008 and 2009 controlled studies give 2x time and 3x success.

source: Parnin and Orso (2011) Are automated debugging techniques actually helping programmers? ISSTA 2011
finding: Known critique that tests assumptions behind fault-localization and slicing tools: that users inspect ranked lists in order and that finding the faulty line means understanding the fault. Not opened this session (PDF not reachable); content is from memory and unverified.
numbers: Not verified. Do not cite figures from this line.
limits: Not read; check the paper before use. Need exact N and which conditions showed no help.
agent_relevance: Important counterweight to Whyline success stories: tool-supplied localization does not guarantee the human or agent understands the cause. Still to be read in the next pass.

source: Ko and Myers (2008) Debugging Reinvented, comparison control group
finding: In the slider bug, most control participants used text search for 'color', which returned 62 matches in 9 files, and others followed data dependencies by hand with breakpoints. Time varied 3 to 38 minutes, mostly from strategy.
numbers: Control median 10 min (range 3-38); 62 matches over 9 files; program about 500 lines with a few inserted bugs.
quote: most used text searches for "color" to find relevant code, revealing 62 matches over 9 files
limits: Control data came from a 2004 study with different conditions (interruptions removed afterwards); cross-study comparison.
agent_relevance: Keyword grep for the symptom is the agent's analogue and gives noisy hits. Backward tracing from the output removes the guess of a search term.

source: Ko and Myers (2004) Designing the Whyline, design guidelines drawn from Alice error study
finding: The authors' earlier study of Alice errors found that half of all errors came from false assumptions in hypotheses made while debugging an existing error, i.e. debugging adds new bugs through wrong guesses. This is the root argument for asking instead of guessing.
numbers: 50% of all errors from false assumptions made in hypotheses during debugging (from their VL/HCC 2003 model of programming errors).
quote: 50% of all errors were due to programmers' false assumptions in the hypotheses they formed while debugging
limits: Cited from a prior study of Alice programmers (novices and experts, contextual and lab settings); not independently replicated here.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 and G2: hypotheses made without evidence create new errors. Agent should hold a hypothesis as a question to be checked against output.

source: Cross-check: Shahandashti et al. (2024) failure taxonomy and prompting fixes
finding: Failure analysis of the wrong LLM slices. Complex control flow was the most common root cause, and most errors sat at variable declarations and assignments. Giving the model feedback about root cause and location and asking it to redo the slice gave only small gains.
numbers: Prompt crafting +4% (GPT-4o), +6.4% GPT-3.5 Turbo, +5.1% Gemma-7B, +2.5% Llama-2; iterative prompting +3.9% for GPT-4o. Failure cases analysed manually: 92 labelled for static slicing.
quote: We identified Complex Control Flow as the most frequent root cause of failures
limits: Manual labelling by the authors; the gains are small and without confidence intervals.
agent_relevance: When the model is the slicer, expect errors at branches and assignments. Give the model a program-analysis tool for this step and keep it for language and explanation.
